title: Turn changing inputs into one useful value
intent: Use this shape when one or two changing facts should produce one value for a view, decision, or outside observer.
public_summary: The smallest useful graph: explicit inputs, one calculation, and one place where the result leaves the graph.

public_sections.heading: A familiar example
body: Quantity and unit price change independently, while the UI needs one total. Make the two facts explicit, derive the total, and let the display observe that result.
bullets: The calculation stays easy to test.
A second consumer can reuse the result without duplicating the logic.

title: Keep a form summary coherent
intent: Use this shape when many fields feed one validation, readiness, or submission decision.
public_summary: Each field can change on its own, while the user should see one summary built from a coherent set of values.

public_sections.heading: Why a graph helps
body: A form is a small fan-in system. Fields arrive and change at different times, but validation, progress, and submit readiness depend on several of them together.
bullets: Keep each field visible as an input.
Do not invent defaults for fields that have not arrived.
Publish one settled summary instead of manually triggering validation from every field.

title: Turn outside events into visible state
intent: Use this shape when events arrive from a browser, socket, device, or host API and should update state inside the graph.
public_summary: Accept an event at a clear boundary, turn it into graph-visible state, and derive the views that depend on it.

public_sections.heading: Keep the handoff clear
body: The browser, device, or host owns when the event occurs. The boundary turns that event into an explicit fact. From there, ordinary graph relationships explain what changes next.
bullets: Keep host callbacks at the boundary.
Derive views from that state rather than triggering them from the callback.

title: Publish a result when the work is complete
intent: Use this shape for imports, bounded streams, batch work, or any report that only makes sense after all input arrives.
public_summary: Collect or reduce input until completion, then publish one final result without polling from the side.

public_sections.heading: Completion is part of the story
body: A final report should be caused by the input completing, not by a timer repeatedly asking whether the work is done. Keeping completion in the flow also gives errors and cleanup a clear place.
bullets: Wait for the bounded input to complete.
Release outside resources at the boundary that owns them.

title: Connect outside work without hiding it
intent: Use this shape for files, network calls, workers, remote graphs, or model calls that finish on their own timing.
public_summary: Let an adapter own the outside operation, then bring its result into the graph as an explicit fact.

public_sections.heading: What the boundary does
body: GraphReFly does not provide network transport. Your application, worker, or adapter performs the outside work. The boundary makes its result visible when it enters the graph, so downstream behavior still has an explainable cause.
bullets: Keep async work in a source, pool, adapter, or bridge.
Publish success, failure, and status explicitly when the product needs them.
Use ordinary graph composition after the result enters.
